Tech Scan: Harness

What runs the agent — the managed harness, the loop frameworks, memory, durable execution and observability around it — and when to use each one.

This page is a draft. It covers the harness only: the loop, tools, memory, safety and observability around an agent. Entries are research references from web sources reviewed 11–12 November 2026, not locally deployed or benchmarked options; qualify any of them in the intended account before adopting it.

Read the harness section of Concepts first — it explains what a harness is and how the agent, its tools and its checks fit together — then use this page to choose the products that implement it.

A note on Tech Scan

Tech Scan is an early exploration of emerging agentic technologies that support the key areas of the AI-SDLC. It is still in its early stages: entries are research references, not settled recommendations, and they may not reflect the latest products or releases. Use your own judgement and do your own research before adopting anything listed here.

Purpose

A harness is the system around the agent: it holds the agent's state, supplies its tools, keeps its memory, runs its loop, enforces its safety rules and records what happened. The guide groups those parts as agent state, tools, memory, orchestration, safety and observability.[1] This page answers which products provide each part, and when the managed default is not enough.

There is no single canonical six. The 2026 framings do not agree on one, and the Tech Scan proposal's list — loop, tools, memory, compute and sandbox, safety, observability — matches none of them exactly.[2][3][22] This page adopts the pillar names from Automater: context assembly, tool design, permissions, memory, evals and observability. Compute and sandbox are the runtime under the pillars, not a pillar themselves, and cost is cross-cutting. The proposal's list omits evaluations (evals) and recovery — the two layers a 60-day production report credits with about 80% of agent stability — so this page covers both: evals as a pillar below, recovery under durable execution.

The six harness pillars
PillarWhat it isAWS-first defaultConditional alternative
Context assemblyStandards, docs and repo state into the promptBedrock Knowledge Bases via AgentCore GatewayQdrant, pgvector or RAGFlow, self-hosted
Tool designTyped tools, MCP servers, approval pointsAgentCore Gateway (MCP tools, Cedar policy)MCP Registry as source of record
PermissionsWho and what the agent may touchAgentCore Policy (Cedar) plus IAMOPA or Conftest (Rego)
MemoryShort-term session and long-term per-user recallAgentCore MemoryMem0, Letta or Graphiti
EvalsOffline and online checks that the agent still worksAgentCore EvaluationsLangfuse, Braintrust or Maxim AI
ObservabilityTraces, token and cost per run, failure replayCloudWatch and AgentCore ObservabilityLangfuse or Arize Phoenix

Context assembly starts from Bedrock Knowledge Bases exposed through AgentCore Gateway.[12][13] Tool design runs through AgentCore Gateway, with Cedar policy governing which tools the agent may call.[11]

What this page does not cover:

  • Model choice (Tech Scan: Models)
  • Retrieval detail (Tech Scan: Context, planned)
  • The execution sandbox (Tech Scan: Sandbox)
  • Gateway routing (Tech Scan: Gateway)

Each is a separate spoke.

AWS-first default

Start with the AgentCore managed harness: a config-based, Strands-powered harness with an explicit approved model, individually allowed tools and bounded execution.[4][5] AWS records its general availability in July 2026.[6] Use managed Claude or OpenAI models through Bedrock; direct provider APIs are exceptions for a specific capability or approved-region gap, not the assumed route. Managed defaults can evolve, so default behaviour is not an immutable model or tool policy — record the exact model, tools and permissions you approved, and review them when the default changes.

For coding work, the managed harness with Code Interpreter is the preferred setup; add the Browser tool only for a specific task, not because both exist. The sandbox must hold six trust rules:[7]

  • Separate trust domains
  • Minimal execution roles
  • Explicit outbound enforcement
  • Approved dependencies
  • Protected credentials
  • Authenticated session ownership

Runtime Instances are not equivalent to per-session microVM compute: co-resident agents in an Instances session share a filesystem and can access each other's execution-role credentials.[8] Gateway policy governs traffic through the Gateway, not arbitrary shell networking. VPC attachment alone is not evidence of package-only egress — network access limited to approved package registries — or secret denial.[7]

Use Step Functions when an outer workflow needs any of these:[9]

  • Explicit sequencing
  • Retries
  • Parallel checks
  • Independently authorised human decisions

Keep that workflow separate from the model's per-turn tool loop.

The optimised InvokeHarness task is request/response only, has a 15-minute task limit, and does not itself support task-token callbacks; a timeout does not automatically cancel the harness.[9][10] Longer work and approval need a separate job or callback design.[9][10]

Conditional alternatives

Use a framework only when the managed configuration cannot express the required behaviour. The managed harness stays the default; a framework is a conditional alternative, not a second stack.

Orchestration frameworks

Orchestration frameworks: the agent loop itself
ProductLicencePick it when
Strands AgentsApache-2.0On AWS: smallest code, MCP-native, runs on AgentCore Runtime
LangGraphMITStateful, long-running work that must pause for a human and resume after failure
CrewAIMITFastest working demo (role-based crews); weaker durable execution
OpenHandsMIT coreSelf-hosted coding agent, closest to the factory loop (issue to pull request)[15]

SmolAgentsApache-2.0Minimal agent (code actions, not JSON tool calls); least support for long-running work

LangGraph has more than compatibility evidence: Thomson Reuters describes its LangGraph-based Aether orchestrator using AgentCore in a customer-coauthored operational case.[14] That remains reported customer evidence, not an independently audited benchmark.[14]

Memory

Memory options
ProductWhat it doesWhen to use it
AgentCore MemoryShort-term session and long-term per-user recall, managedDefault; use unless a specific memory behaviour needs a separate store
Mem0 (Apache-2.0)Long-term memory layer for agentsWhen the managed memory cannot express the required recall behaviour

Zep stopped maintaining its open-source Community Edition in April 2025 — self-host Graphiti, not Zep.[23]

Durable execution

Durable execution is for agents that wait hours or days for approval, or must survive crashes. The platform-native option is Bedrock AgentCore itself; the options below are for work the managed harness cannot carry.

Durable execution options
ProductWhat it doesWhen to use it
TemporalDurable execution engineAgents that wait hours or days for approval, or must survive crashes
InngestEvent-driven durable executionAgents that wait hours or days for approval, or must survive crashes
Trigger.dev (Apache-2.0)Durable executionAgents that wait hours or days for approval, or must survive crashes
Hatchet (MIT)Durable task executionAgents that wait hours or days for approval, or must survive crashes
Restate, DBOS or PrefectDurable executionAgents that wait hours or days for approval, or must survive crashes

Trigger.dev carries a caveat: on 1 November 2026 Trigger.dev disclosed that an attacker reached environment variables for a subset of customer organisations on its hosted tier, so verify the hosted tier before recommending it.[24]

Evals and observability

Observability defaults to CloudWatch and AgentCore Observability.[16][17] Check whether CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights covers Claude Code and Codex before adding another platform: its ready-made dashboards depend on the expected telemetry names and resource attributes.[17]

Evals and observability options
ProductWhat it doesWhen to use it
AgentCore EvaluationsOffline and online checks that the agent still worksDefault for evals
CloudWatch and AgentCore ObservabilityTraces, token and cost per run, failure replayDefault for observability
Langfuse (MIT core)LLM-native traces, prompt versioning, eval scoringWhen prompt, version and evaluation workflows justify another platform
BraintrustEval-driven development, trace-to-test loopWhen eval workflows justify another platform
Maxim AIConversation simulation and evalsWhen eval workflows justify another platform
Arize Phoenix (Elastic Licence 2.0, source-available, not OSI open source; now Dynatrace)Traces and evals for agentsWhen an observability alternative to CloudWatch is needed

Langfuse has the strongest public AWS evidence among the alternatives: official AWS deployment documentation and the vendor's report of using ECS Fargate for its own application.[18][20] Distinguish the deployment paths: the current official Terraform module provisions EKS/Fargate, not the same ECS setup.[19]

A LangChain survey of 1,340 practitioners (November–December 2025) found 89% have some AI observability, but only 52.4% run offline evals and 37.3% run online evals on live traffic.[22] Evals are the immature half of this section: budget for them as a practice, not only as a tool.

MCP registries

The official MCP Registry is the source of record for MCP servers; Glama is the vetting layer.[21] Smithery's proxy and managed identity shut down on 31 October 2026 — migrate any server.smithery.ai URL to the vendor's direct MCP URL.[21] Mintlify is a docs platform with a hosted MCP server, not a registry.[21]

Research-only notes

The pillar names on this page are adopted from Automater, not canonical.[2] The heyuan110 framing names a different six, built around execution and recovery rather than permissions and observability, and credits evaluation and recovery with about 80% of agent stability in one 60-day production report.[3]

The memory and durable-execution alternatives above are research references, not locally tested options. The research gives no named AWS operational case for them, so they stay conditional alternatives: options to qualify, not defaults to adopt.

The MCP registry landscape is still forming: the official registry as source of record and Glama as vetting layer correct older guidance that named Smithery or Mintlify as registries.

Do not use

Do not start new work on any of these. They appear here so a team inheriting them recognises them as retired, not as live options.[22]

  • AutoGen — archived by Microsoft, with no fixes. The live community fork is AG2.
  • Semantic Kernel — in maintenance mode.
  • OpenAI Assistants API — removed on 26 August 2026.
  • LangChain AgentExecutor — deprecated, end of life December 2026.

Gaps and open questions

Managed defaults can evolve, so default behaviour is not an immutable model or tool policy. Record the approved model, tools and permissions for each harness, and review them when the default changes.

No option on this page has been locally deployed or benchmarked. Every entry is a documentation or source review; qualification is still to be done in the intended account:

  • Representative task success
  • Permission revocation
  • Timeouts and retries
  • Full cost

Recovery has no single home in the pillar framing. It is spread across Step Functions retries, durable execution and the harness's own bounded execution. If recovery becomes a first-class requirement, give it its own pillar rather than stretching the six.

The InvokeHarness limit leaves a gap for long work and approvals: no managed approval-callback pattern is named in the research. A team that needs human approval inside a run needs to design the job or callback itself.

Next step: read the harness section in Concepts, then qualify the managed default in the intended account (see the checks above) before adopting it for production work.
